meta.title: Vietnamese A1 Learning Data — Southern (Saigon) Dialect
meta.description: Vocabulary and grammar dataset behind the 'Bé Rồng' learning app and matching PDF cheat sheet. Contains 75 adjectives, 75 verbs, 75 nouns, 30 core grammar cards, plus directions/prepositions and Southern pronunciation notes that currently exist only in the PDF (not yet in the app).

grammar_core.note: muốn + verb = 'want to do something'.
có thể + verb = 'can/could'. Often paired with 'không?' to ask.

grammar_core.sEn: I have to go to work early.
grammar_core.note: phải + verb = obligation, 'must/have to'.
nên + verb = gentle advice, 'should'.

grammar_core.sEn: I need a glass of water.
grammar_core.note: cần + noun/verb = 'need'.

grammar_core.sEn: This one is bigger than that one.
grammar_core.note: Comparative: adjective + hơn + noun = 'more ___ than'.

grammar_core.sEn: This is the most delicious dish.
grammar_core.note: Superlative: adjective + nhất = 'the most ___'.

grammar_core.sEn: I am as tall as you.
grammar_core.note: Equal comparison: adjective + bằng + noun = 'as ___ as'.

grammar_core.en: less than / not as good as
grammar_core.sEn: I sing worse than my older sister.
grammar_core.note: kém + noun = 'not as good as / worse than'.
đã + verb = completed/past action.

grammar_core.sEn: I am studying Vietnamese right now.
grammar_core.note: đang + verb = action happening now.

grammar_core.sEn: Tomorrow I will go to work.
grammar_core.note: sẽ + verb = future action.
không + verb/adjective = general negation.
chưa + verb = 'not yet'; also 'đã ... chưa?' = 'have you ... yet?'

grammar_core.sEn: What do you want to eat?
grammar_core.note: 'gì' (what) goes at the end of the phrase it refers to.
'ai' (who) can start or end a sentence.
'ở đâu' (where) usually comes at the end of the sentence.
'khi nào' can start the sentence for future events.
'tại sao' starts the question; answers often use 'vì' (because).
'thế nào' asks about quality or manner, placed at the end.
'bao nhiêu' asks about quantity or price.
Classifier 'con' is used before animals (and casually for some people).
Classifier 'cái' is used before most inanimate objects.
Classifier 'quyển' (or 'cuốn') is used before books/notebooks.
'của' shows possession: noun + của + owner.
'làm ơn' politely softens a request, placed before the verb.
'hãy' before a verb makes a polite suggestion or command.
'đừng' + verb = negative command, 'don't do that'.
'rất' goes before the adjective.
Southern colloquial 'quá' after the adjective emphasizes it strongly.

southern_accent_pronunciation_notes: gi-, d-, v- are all pronounced like the English 'y' in the South (giá, da, và all start with the same /y/ sound) — in the North they're kept distinct.
r is a true 'r' sound in the South (like English 'r'); in the North it often sounds like 'z'.
The hỏi (˧˩˧) and ngã (˧ˀ˥) tones are usually merged into one tone in casual Southern speech, while Northern speech keeps them distinct.
Final -n/-ng and -t/-c often blur together in fast Southern speech (e.g. 'ăn' can sound close to 'ăng') — don't worry if you can't hear the difference at first.
Southerners say dạ for a polite 'yes'/acknowledgment far more often than vâng (which is more Northern); very casually, 'không' is often shortened to hông or hổng.
